title: What Are the Parts of an HVAC System?
h1: What Are the Main Parts of an HVAC System, and What Does Each One Do?
description: Learn the main parts of a home HVAC system, from the furnace and outdoor unit to ducts, coils, filters and the thermostat, and what each part does.
quick_answer: A typical home HVAC system has a heating unit (a furnace or heat pump), an outdoor condenser for cooling, an indoor evaporator coil, a blower that moves air, ductwork with supply and return vents, a filter, a condensate drain and a thermostat that tells everything when to run. Each part depends on the others to keep air moving.
body:
Most homes in San Diego and Orange County have a split system. That means some equipment sits outside, some sits inside, and copper refrigerant lines and wiring connect the two. Inside, the furnace or air handler is usually in the attic, the garage or a hall closet, and the ducts run through the attic to each room.

Knowing the basic parts helps you describe a problem clearly, understand a repair estimate and spot trouble early. Here's how it all fits together.

What does the heating side include?

In most local homes, heat comes from a gas furnace or an electric heat pump.

  • Burners and igniter. A gas furnace lights its burners with a hot surface igniter or spark. A flame sensor confirms the flame is there, or the furnace shuts the gas off.
  • Heat exchanger. The flame heats this metal chamber, and house air passes over the outside of it. The combustion gases stay inside and leave through the flue, which is why a cracked heat exchanger is a safety concern.
  • Flue or vent pipe. This carries combustion gases outside. It has to stay connected and clear.
  • Heat pump. A heat pump looks like an AC unit outside but can run in reverse to move heat into the house. Many newer homes and remodels use one instead of a gas furnace.

What parts handle the cooling?

Central air works by moving heat from inside your home to outside. Four parts do most of the work.

  • Outdoor condenser. This is the box beside your house. It holds the compressor, which pumps refrigerant, plus a coil and a fan that release heat outdoors.
  • Evaporator coil. This coil usually sits on top of the furnace or inside the air handler. Cold refrigerant runs through it, and the blower pushes warm house air across it.
  • Refrigerant lines. Two copper lines carry refrigerant between the indoor coil and the outdoor unit. The larger one is insulated and feels cool when the AC runs.
  • Metering device. A small valve controls how much refrigerant enters the indoor coil.

Refrigerant work requires special training and equipment, so leave that part to a technician.

How does air get to every room?

The blower is a fan inside the furnace or air handler. It pulls air in through the return grille, pushes it through the filter and across the coil or heat exchanger, and sends it out through the supply ducts.

The ductwork is the network that carries that air. Supply ducts end at the registers in each room. Return ducts bring air back to the system, often through one or two large grilles in a hallway or ceiling. In attic installs, ducts sit in a space that can get very hot in summer, so leaks and torn insulation waste a lot of the air you paid to cool. Our air duct services cover cleaning, sealing and repair.

What do the filter, drain and thermostat do?

These smaller parts cause a surprising number of service calls.

  • Air filter. It catches dust and debris before they reach the blower and coil. A clogged filter chokes airflow and can cause the AC coil to freeze or the furnace to overheat.
  • Condensate drain. Cooling pulls moisture out of the air. That water drips into a pan under the coil and leaves through a drain line. If the line clogs, water can back up into the attic or closet ceiling.
  • Thermostat. This is the control center. It tells the furnace, blower and outdoor unit when to start and stop. Some thermostats also control humidity accessories or zones.
  • Electrical parts. Capacitors, contactors, relays and the control board handle starting and stopping. A weak capacitor is a common reason an outdoor unit hums but won't start.

Which parts wear out first?

In our experience, the parts that need attention most often are the simple ones. Filters get skipped, drain lines clog with algae, capacitors weaken in hot weather and flame sensors get dirty. Outdoor coils near the coast can also corrode faster because of salt air, and coils in dusty inland areas clog with dirt and leaves.

A yearly tune-up checks all of these before they turn into a no-heat or no-cool call. If you're not sure how old your system is or which parts you have, our team can take a look during a visit. You can read more about repairs and replacements on our HVAC services page.

What can a homeowner check safely?

You don't need tools to keep an eye on the basics:

  1. Check the filter every month and replace it when it looks gray or dusty.
  2. Keep plants, fences and stored items a couple of feet away from the outdoor unit.
  3. Make sure supply registers and the return grille aren't blocked by furniture or rugs.
  4. Look for water around the furnace or air handler, or stains on the ceiling below an attic unit.
  5. Note any new noises, smells or short cycling and tell your technician.

Leave gas valves, electrical panels and refrigerant lines alone. If you ever smell gas, leave the house and call your gas utility from outside. If a carbon monoxide alarm goes off, get everyone out and call 911.
faqs: Where is the furnace usually located in a Southern California home?

Most furnaces here are in the attic, the garage or a hall closet. Homes in this area rarely have basements, so attic installs with ducts running through the attic are very common, especially in single-story tract homes.
What is the difference between an air handler and a furnace?

Both contain a blower that moves air through your ducts. A furnace also makes heat by burning gas. An air handler has no burner and is usually paired with a heat pump, sometimes with electric heat strips for backup.
Can one part fail and shut down the whole system?
Yes. A clogged condensate drain can trip a safety switch, a bad capacitor can stop the outdoor unit and a dirty flame sensor can keep a furnace from staying lit. Small parts often cause big symptoms.
How long do HVAC systems usually last?

It depends on the equipment, how it was installed and how well it has been maintained. Coastal salt air and long inland cooling seasons both add wear. A technician can tell you more about your system's condition during an inspection.
